newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire army reports battle on road to 3rd city.
newsitem.headline: Zaire army reports battle on road to 3rd city.

text.p: Zaire's army said on Friday it had won a fierce battle with rebels for a key bridge on the main road to its third city of Kisangani, its military headquarters for the civil war in the east.
A senior defence ministry official told Reuters at the same time the army was reinforcing Kisangani with 2,000 battle-hardened paratroops from its 31st brigade near the capital Kinshasa.
"Rotations have started between Kinshasa and Kisangani. Soldiers from the valiant 31st brigade are being gradually ferried to Kisangani which has become a fortress," he said.

The official said the rebels, who have announced their intention to capture Kisangani, were attacking on several fronts across the eastern war zone to draw the army away from the strategic city on the mighty Zaire River.
He said the battle for the bridge on the Osso River near Lubutu, 200 km (125 miles) southeast of Kisangani, had taken place on Wednesday evening.
"These clashes killed more than 30 of the enemy who fled. They have pulled back a long way," he added, noting that the latest news from the battlefront was not so alarming.
The official rejected rebel suggestions the army was using napalm: "It's untrue. Zaire has never used napalm in this war."
He acknowledged the army had used napalm to curb a revolt in the mineral-rich southern province of Shaba in the 1970s. "But that brought condemnation from the international community," he said.
The official said the army had retaken Bafwasende in the northeast while rebels had taken Faradje in the northeast corner of the country near Sudan -- in both cases without a fight.

"There was no fighting in Bafwasende. When the army arrived there the rebels had already left. Likewise in Faradje, which is now in rebel hands, there was no fighting. The rebels moved in after the departure of our troops," he added.
Ethnic Tutsis launched the war in October accusing Zairean authorities of denying them citizenship and planning to expel them to neighbouring Rwanda, their ancestral home.

Rebel leader Laurent Kabila said after the fall of Isiro, 340 km (210 miles) northeast of Kisangani, that ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko's jungle palace at Gbadolite was a target -- although this is hundreds of kilometres (miles) from the front.
Kabila has given Mobutu, who had prostate surgery in Europe in August, until February 21 to begin talks on stepping down.

Rebel activity around Lubutu has led to an exodus of Zaireans from nearby villages. Almost 200,000 trapped Rwandan Hutu refugee are clustered around the nearby village of Tingi Tingi but Kabila has ordered his forces to avoid the camp.

U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan said on Thursday dropping plans for an international force to rescue refugees in eastern Zaire had been premature. He told a news conference in New York it would have been better to suspend the plans in order to activate them later if needed.
"In the absence of the willing and the will, there is little the United Nations can do in terms of putting in a force to help stranded refugees," he said.
